raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils, leading to ventricular thickening, diastolic dysfunction, restrictive physiology, arrhythmias, conduction disease, and eventually advanced heart failure. Although many precursor proteins can form amyloid, clinically important cardiac disease is dominated by immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL) and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), the latter occurring as wild-type ATTR or hereditary/variant ATTR [1,2]. AL cardiac amyloidosis is a hematologic emergency because circulating monoclonal light chains are directly cardiotoxic and rapid clone-directed therapy can be life-saving [3]. ATTR cardiomyopathy, once considered rare, is now recognized as a common underdiagnosed cause of heart failure in older adults, especially men, and is increasingly identified because of noninvasive scintigraphic diagnosis and disease-modifying therapy [4]. Contemporary scientific statements and position papers emphasize early suspicion, accurate amyloid typing, and multidisciplinary management [5,6].

The clinical phenotype is heterogeneous. AL disease often presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria, autonomic dysfunction, macroglossia, periorbital purpura, or rapidly progressive heart failure, whereas ATTR commonly presents as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, low-flow aortic stenosis, conduction disease, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, or biceps tendon rupture. Comparative cohorts show that AL, hereditary ATTR, and wild-type ATTR have distinct clinical courses and prognoses [7]. Wild-type ATTR typically affects older adults and has better untreated survival than AL, although outcomes remain poor once heart failure is established [8-10]. Screening studies have identified ATTR among patients labeled as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, severe calcific aortic stenosis, and those undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement [11-13]. Recognition of extracardiac “red flags,” especially carpal tunnel syndrome preceding cardiac diagnosis by years, can prompt earlier testing [14].

Diagnosis begins with clinical suspicion in a patient with increased ventricular wall thickness, unexplained heart failure, discordant low or normal electrocardiographic voltage, persistent troponin elevation, apical-sparing strain, or characteristic cardiac magnetic resonance findings. Echocardiography commonly demonstrates concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, valve thickening, restrictive filling, small stroke volume, and reduced global longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance provides tissue characterization with diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal nulling, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume; these features are diagnostic and prognostic [16,17]. Bone-avid tracer scintigraphy with technetium-labeled pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP distinguishes ATTR from AL when interpreted carefully [18]. In patients with typical cardiac imaging, grade 2 or 3 scintigraphic uptake, and no monoclonal protein by serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation, ATTR cardiomyopathy can be diagnosed without biopsy [19]. However, any monoclonal gammopathy requires tissue confirmation and amyloid typing, ideally by mass spectrometry, because AL and ATTR can coexist and treatment differs fundamentally.

Risk stratification is biomarker centered. In AL amyloidosis, cardiac troponin, natriuretic peptides, and the difference between involved and uninvolved free light chains define stage and prognosis [20]. Hematologic response is assessed by free light-chain suppression, while cardiac response is commonly tracked by natriuretic peptide reduction and symptoms [21]. First-line therapy for newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis has shifted toward daratumumab plus cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone, which improves hematologic complete response rates; selected fit patients may still be considered for autologous stem-cell transplantation after expert evaluation [22]. Supportive cardiac care relies on meticulous volume control, salt restriction, and loop diuretics; conventional heart-failure neurohormonal therapies are often poorly tolerated because of fixed stroke volume, hypotension, renal dysfunction, and autonomic involvement.

ATTR therapy targets transthyretin stabilization or production. Tafamidis, a TTR tetramer stabilizer, reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization in ATTR cardiomyopathy and remains a foundational therapy for symptomatic patients with preserved functional status [23]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer designed for near-complete TTR stabilization, improved a hierarchical composite outcome in ATTR cardiomyopathy [24]. Gene-silencing therapies have expanded the field: vutrisiran reduced death and recurrent cardiovascular events in ATTR cardiomyopathy, while patisiran improved functional and quality-of-life endpoints in cardiac ATTR and previously showed benefit in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [25-27]. Inotersen is effective for hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy but requires monitoring for thrombocytopenia and glomerulonephritis [28]. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 TTR editing has shown proof-of-concept for durable TTR reduction, but long-term safety and cardiac outcome data are still evolving [29]. Current care therefore requires early diagnosis, genetic testing for all ATTR cases, family counseling for pathogenic variants, longitudinal biomarker and functional monitoring, and coordinated cardiology, hematology, neurology, nephrology, and palliative-care expertise [30].
